# Unmarked Exits

Consider the last time you were carried.

Not the best time, or the scariest, or the funniest—the *last*. Someone's arms, someone's hip, the whole world viewed from above waist height. Statistically, this event certainly occurred: nearly every ambulatory human passes through it. And no one marked it. Your parents set you down a final time with the same absent-minded care as the ten thousand previous times, muttering about dinner, and neither of you knew that a door had just swung shut in another room. No photograph was taken. No entry was made. The occasion occurred inside you and outside your notice simultaneously, and now it is permanently beyond retrieval—the precise afternoon is gone, the weather on that afternoon is gone, the exact weight you were when weight stopped mattering is gone.

We are a civilization with an enormous bureaucracy devoted to firsts. Baby books contain printed slots for them: first smile, first tooth, first step, first word, each awaiting a date and a proud pen. Schools Photograph the first day annually against the same front door. Every language has festive machinery for beginnings. But manufacture me a book with a ruled space at the bottom that says *last time carried, weight unknown.* The publishing industry has not attempted it, because there is nothing anyone could write in the box. Firsts wave at us from the windshield. Lasts ride silently in the trunk.

How, then, do we ever discover them? Only from the far side. You learn that a certain evening was final at a funeral, or a demolition, or a garage sale, or an awkward unanswered message, and retroactively the bookkeeping begins: so that was it, that Tuesday, that walk to the car. Life files its paperwork in arrears. Kierkegaard said it plainly more than a century and a half ago—we live life forwards but understand it backwards—and lasts are the purest demonstration. Their significance is awarded late, like a grade posted after the course has ended and everyone has gone home.

Most lasts, in fact, will never be graded at all, because most are too small for anyone to conduct the investigation. Consider the inventory. Almost every adult took a final cartwheel and did not report it to authorities; the body simply stopped offering, and the mind didn't subpoena the moment. There's a pencil you owned that slipped out of a jacket pocket somewhere in the world and has been lying in that grass ever since, unclaimed by your conscious life—its last day of duty passed without memo. Your handwriting changed forever somewhere in adolescence, a border crossing nobody witnessed or stamped. Whole vocabularies die in single mouths: you pronounced some word wrong as a child—*aminal, liberry, pasghetti*—someone corrected it gently, and that pronunciation was never uttered again anywhere in the universe. Old parents sometimes grieve those little extinctions years afterward, the way one misses a bird call from a vanished yard. Even slang retires without ceremony. A season came when you stopped saying some once-beloved bit of nonsense, and no one held a briefing.

Friendships perform the same vanishing act at scale. At sixteen, everyone says *see you Monday* with total sincerity, and mostly it's true—Monday arrives, then hundreds more Mondays—and then one specific Friday in a paneled basement, amid couches and cheap pizza, turns out to be the final gathering of that particular five people in the history of the planet. There was no slow motion. There was no music cue. Everyone drove home mildly bored and hopeful, which may be the strangest detail of all: unawareness doesn't feel like anything. It feels like a Tuesday. Decades later somebody half-jokes about a reunion that will not happen, and everyone agrees enthusiastically, and that agreement is itself the tombstone being laid.

Places do it too. The pool where you spent entire childhood summers is a parking structure now, and therefore you personally attended the pool's final performance as an audience of one, without applauding. The diner is a bank. Your grandmother's kitchen was sold along with the house and behaves as someone else's sunroom. Even songs: there is an album you played flat-out one entire summer—there is exactly one such album, and you could name it in half a second if pressed—and sometime afterwards, without trial, you heard it for the last time. Nothing banned it. The seasons simply transferred possession of you.

Here is where the melancholy starts to seem like a design flaw. We assign meaning backward because that is the only direction understanding can travel; significance requires comparison, and comparison requires elapsed distance. Fair enough. But science hints the backwardness goes deeper than philosophy. The neuroscientist David Eagleman tells of experiments in which people glimpse flashes of images, and when a frightening picture flickers by, it seems to run long—fear stretches the instant. His suggestion, wonderfully counterintuitive, is that the brain sends word *backwards*, reaching into the preceding fraction of a second to pack it with extra memory, the way the cartoon Slinky Dog stretches his rear half backward while his front half bolts ahead. Take the detail with appropriate scientific salt. But relish the image: surprise recruits the recent past, pads it, densifies it. Which means significance, even in the skull, is applied after the fact, smuggled in through a door once the moment has already left the building. No wonder lasts escape us. The alarm rings only after the visitor has driven off.

So is the concealment cruelty or mercy?

Try the alternative. Imagine receiving notification. Every interaction date-stamped: FINAL EDITION. Grief would arrive years early and take the chair beside you at breakfast, pre-mourning the living across the table while the toast cools. Hugging a friend would mean scanning her face for archival purposes while missing whatever she was saying. Ordinary life is load-bearing; bolt commemorative plaques to every beam and the floor collapses. Suppose every bedtime tuck-in arrived labeled *among these is the last*—which one, parent, do you guess? The guessing would ruin all of them. Suspense withheld may be the kindest effect consciousness ever produced.

And yet complete amnesia has its own cost, and most of us sense it. The Japanese aesthetic tradition folds transience directly into beauty—*mono no aware*, the gentle ache of things passing—and treats the brevity of cherry blossoms not as a defect but as the reason for the pilgrimage. The Stoics ran drills: rehearse the loss of what you love, Seneca advised, not to invite disaster but to raise the deductible of taking it for granted. Used as seasoning, imagining absence concentrates presence remarkably. Modern parenting even circulates the rumor informally: someone tells a new father, *one day you'll pick her up and never pick her up again,* and you can watch the man start hoisting his toddler slower and longer that very week, one handed-down dose of mortality administered orally, improving vision.

Notice, too, what happens wherever context manages to announce a last despite the general secrecy. In hospice work, where ends are met face to face, people perform them deliberately and tenderly: one more drive with the windows down, a favorite record played twice, the preferred dessert for no stated reason. Wrecking crews pause before the swing of the crane. Even small仪式 invented impromptu—crew members patting a wall of a building that housed forty years of lives—suggest the instinct is abundance everywhere, merely starved of dispatch information elsewhere. Reverence was never the shortage. Data was.

Language itself confesses the problem. *Farewell* began as travel well; Spanish speakers still commend each other to God in *adiós*; English squeezed *God be with ye* down to *goodbye*, an entire blessing contracted for portability. Which points to something genuinely unprecedented about being alive now. Every generation before ours lost its lasts completely—to dust, to distance, to burned letters, to water damage, to plain forgetfulness. You cannot excavate what was never recorded. Today's bereaved, by contrast, dig wells instead of gullies: the last voicemail preserved with religious care, unsent-to-delete because deletion means the voice finally dies; the final text thread scrolled upward by flashlight; the last photograph where she is laughing at somebody's wedding, its timestamp functioning as a headstone engraving. An archive remembers timestamps, never temperatures; it preserves the sentence but not the soup steam rising behind it. The danger is mistaking the artifact for an interview. Its purpose is the person, not the prosecution.

What follows practically? Not the standard prescription. *Live each day as your last* sounds noble and lands badly—in execution it produces mostly insomnia, liquidated savings, and tearful confessions to bewildered baristas. A gentler instrument exists, and it's grammatical: the future perfect. *This will have been.* Once a day, maybe, look up from the middle of some unredeemably ordinary scene—porch, June, the sprinkler ticking back and forth while someone explains lawn care at excessive length—and file it forward: *someday I will remember this exact unremarkable hum as paradise.* Stamp the letter now so the past receives it properly sorted later. The operation takes eight seconds and costs nothing but attention, and it converts dread into bookkeeping. You are not predicting doom. You are paying respect in advance to the probable finitude of the unglamorous, which is where ninety-five percent of love actually resides.

Apply it to the largest things first. Hold the child and register the weight as fact rather than forecast: the density, the shampoo, the heel kicking your forearm. Somewhere inside the long sequence of lifts is, yes, a terminal pickup, hidden like one smooth pebble in acres of sand. You will never sift every hug to find it; that way madness lies. Instead handle every stone you're given as though it could be—which is free, and pays forever. Call the grandmother on a random Thursday, not a calendared holiday, precisely *because* Thursday refuses to declare its intentions. Eat lunch outside in October on purpose. Wear the good shirt on no occasion whatsoever, thereby manufacturing an occasion retroactively.

Because here is the truth worth keeping in a coat pocket: the lasts have all sent regrets; they will attend none of our events. The invitations read *regrets only,* and the mailbox stays silent. What remains addressable is the present—the sole venue still admitting guests tonight. So do the arithmetic honestly. No one knows which goodbye is real, which argues for making all of them careless—not careless in spirit, careless in ceremony: full, undecorated, ordinary in form but packed to the seams in content, like a glass you'd fill high for a guest you might never host again without breathing a word about the odds.

And when a small person next throws both arms toward you—that gesture finite, its final member already determined yet unpublished—bend down. Lift. Note the genuine weight of an unbudgeted, one-of-a-kind, rapidly depreciating edition, and hold it accordingly, reading the fine print you wrote yourself just now: *this will have been.* Then set it down gently, the way you'd set down anything valuable whose remaining supply you've decided not to look up.

3. A philosophical meditation
4. A piece about something in the world—nature, cities, technology

Let me write about... maybe "the hour before dawn" or "walking at night" or "the life of a small thing." Or perhaps something about attention itself—the way we see or fail to see. Or the strange experience of remembering.

- Waiting rooms
- The sound of rain
- Lost things
- The last time you do something (you never know when it's the last time)
